what_it_does: A hardware prefetcher is a circuit that tries to guess which data a processor will need next and fetches it from slower memory in advance, so the processor does not have to wait. Existing prefetchers for "spatial" access patterns — where a program tends to use a cluster of nearby memory locations together — make their guesses by looking at which instruction triggered the access or what the address was, but these external clues often fail to generalize across different programs. This paper's system, called Gaze, instead looks at the internal structure of the access pattern itself: specifically, the order in which individual cache lines (small fixed-size chunks of memory) are touched within a region. The idea is that the temporal ordering of accesses within a region is a more reliable fingerprint of how the program actually uses memory. For very dense access patterns where almost everything in a region gets touched, Gaze applies a two-stage filter to avoid fetching data that will be read anyway without any advance work needed.
